Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)  -- A roadside bombing in Somalia's capital killed 21 women who were cleaning rubbish from a southern Mogadishu street on Sunday morning, a hospital official said. Mogadishu residents gather around victims of the bomb attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road. The bomb blast wounded another 46 people, most of them Somali women who had gathered to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in southern Mogadishu's Kilometer 4 district, according to Medina Hospital director Dr. Dahir Dhere. "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area," said witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." "They were innocent poor mothers or sisters," Gedi said. "Why did they deserve this?" It is unclear who is behind the attack. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently fired by the country's prime minister, blamed the Islamic Courts Union for waging the attack. But the head of the Islamist insurgent group, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, denied any involvement and blamed Somalia's government for orchestrating the attack. The victims were participating in a program that allows Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The United Nations' World Food Program organized the program, which began last year and is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority. Mogadishu has been the site of violence in recent months between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's current transitional government is trying to maintain control of the capital, with the help of the better-equipped Ethiopian forces. On Saturday, two-thirds of the Somali government ministers announced their resignations, blaming Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," which they said included his firing of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade said he suspects the mass resignations were aimed at weakening implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He said he had no plans to resign. The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Court Union which overthrew the government in 2006. The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia's transitional government. If followed, the peace deal would pave the way for a withdrawal of Ethiopian troops -- a major sticking point for Islamist fighters who oppose their presence. The agreement calls on the alliance to dissociate itself from armed groups still fighting the government and for all sides to allow "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somalis. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will monitor the agreement's implementation. Ethiopian forces became embroiled in an Islamist insurgency after the Ethiopian forces invaded Somalia in December 2006 to overthrow the ICU leaders and reinstall the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks mounted, efforts to replace the Ethiopians with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission faltered. Ethiopia's invasion had the blessing of Somalia's government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring fugitives from the al Qaeda terrorist movement. The conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, further worsening a humanitarian crisis that dates back to the collapse of the country's last government in 1991. The situation has been exacerbated by drought, continual armed conflicts in central and southern Somalia, and high inflation on food and fuel prices. CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN) -- A roadside bomb in Somalia's capital killed 21 women on Sunday morning as they were clearing rubbish from a street in southern Mogadishu, according to a hospital official. Residents gathered around the victims of the attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road.

The blast also wounded 46 others, most of them Somali women who had assembled to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in the Kilometer 4 district of southern Mogadishu, said Dr. Dahir Dhere, director of Medina Hospital.

"It suddenly turned the area into a scene of carnage, scattering the body parts of the street cleaners across a wide area," recalled witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never witnessed such mass killing."

"They were innocent, poor mothers and sisters," Gedi added. "Why did they deserve this?"

The identity of those responsible for the attack remains unknown. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently dismissed by the country's prime minister, attributed the bombing to the Islamic Courts Union. However, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, leader of the Islamist insurgent group, denied any involvement and instead accused Somalia's government of orchestrating the attack.

The victims had been participating in a program allowing Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The initiative, launched last year by the United Nations' World Food Program, is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority.

Mogadishu has endured months of violence stemming from clashes between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's transitional government continues to strive for control of the capital, aided by the better-equipped Ethiopian forces.

On Saturday, two-thirds of Somalia's government ministers announced their resignations, denouncing what they described as the "dictatorship" of Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade—citing, among other grievances, his dismissal of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade suggested that the mass resignations were intended to undermine implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He stated he has no intention of resigning.

The peace agreement, signed on June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia—an opposition coalition that includes members of the Islamic Courts Union, which had overthrown the government in 2006 before being ousted later that year by Ethiopian forces with the backing of Somalia's transitional government.

If honored, the agreement would pave the way for the withdrawal of Ethiopian troops, a major point of contention for Islamist fighters opposed to their presence. The deal also requires the alliance to distance itself from armed groups still resisting the government and calls on all parties to permit "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to the Somali people. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will oversee the agreement's implementation.

Ethiopian forces became entangled in an Islamist insurgency after invading Somalia in December 2006 to depose the Islamic Courts Union's leadership and restore the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks intensified, efforts to replace Ethiopian troops with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission stalled.

Ethiopia's invasion was sanctioned by both Somalia's government and the United States, which had accused the Islamic Courts Union of harboring al Qaeda fugitives. The ensuing conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, deepening a humanitarian crisis that has persisted since the collapse of the country's government in 1991. The situation has been further aggravated by drought, ongoing armed conflict in central and southern Somalia, and soaring food and fuel prices.

CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

# Roadside Bomb Kills 21 Female Street Sweepers in Mogadishu

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN) -- Twenty-one women lost their lives Sunday morning when an explosive device detonated along a roadway in Somalia's capital city, according to a hospital administrator. The victims had been engaged in trash removal work on a street in southern Mogadishu.

Local residents crowded around the casualties near Maka Al Mukarama Road following the explosion. Dr. Dahir Dhere, who directs Medina Hospital, reported that the blast also injured 46 additional people—the majority being Somali women who had assembled to clear debris from the road in the Kilometer 4 area of southern Mogadishu.

Eyewitness Asha Ise Gedi described the horrific aftermath: "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area. There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." She questioned the senselessness of the attack, noting the victims were simply "innocent poor mothers or sisters" who didn't deserve such a fate.

The identity of those responsible remains unknown. Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who had served as Mogadishu's mayor before being dismissed by the prime minister, pointed fingers at the Islamic Courts Union. However, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, leader of that Islamist insurgent organization, rejected these accusations and instead accused the Somali government of staging the attack.

These women had been participants in a food-for-work initiative allowing Somalis to earn meals through street-cleaning labor. The United Nations World Food Program launched this program last year, with Mogadishu's regional government overseeing its administration.

## Ongoing Political Turmoil

The Somali capital has recently witnessed clashes between Ethiopian military forces and Islamist combatants. The transitional government currently governing Somalia relies on assistance from the more heavily armed Ethiopian troops to retain control over the capital.

A day earlier, on Saturday, the majority of Somalia's cabinet ministers—roughly two-thirds—tendered their resignations. They accused Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade of authoritarian behavior, specifically citing his removal of Mogadishu's mayor as evidence of this "dictatorship."

Nur Ade suggested that the coordinated resignations were designed to undermine progress on the peace accord between the transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He stated firmly that he had no intention of stepping down.

## Background on the Peace Agreement

Signed on June 9 in Djibouti, the peace accord establishes a cease-fire between Somalia's UN-backed transitional government and the ARS opposition coalition, which includes former members of the Islamic Courts Union—the group that had seized control of the government in 2006 before being driven out by Ethiopian military intervention later that year, backed by the transitional government.

Should the agreement hold, it would create conditions for Ethiopian troop withdrawal, addressing a key grievance among Islamist fighters opposed to their continued presence. The deal also requires the alliance to distance itself from militant groups still battling government forces, while mandating that all parties permit unrestricted humanitarian aid access throughout Somalia. Implementation will be tracked by a joint oversight committee headed by United Nations representatives.

## Roots of the Conflict

Ethiopian troops found themselves caught in an Islamist rebellion after invading Somalia in December 2006 with the goal of toppling ICU leadership and restoring the transitional government. As insurgent attacks intensified, attempts to transition security responsibilities to an African Union peacekeeping force struggled to gain traction.

Both the Somali government and the United States endorsed Ethiopia's military intervention at the time, with American officials alleging that the ICU was providing safe haven to al Qaeda operatives. The resulting conflict forced hundreds of thousands of Somalis from their homes, compounding a humanitarian emergency that has persisted since the previous government's collapse in 1991. Drought conditions, persistent fighting throughout central and southern regions, and soaring costs for food and fuel have further intensified the crisis.

*CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.*

# Deadly Roadside Bombing Kills 21 Women in Mogadishu

A devastating roadside bomb attack in Mogadishu has claimed the lives of 21 women and left 46 others wounded, marking one of the deadliest single incidents to strike civilians in the war-torn Somali capital in recent months. The explosion occurred on Maka Al Mukarama Road, targeting a group of women who were engaged in what should have been a routine humanitarian activity—cleaning the city's streets.

## Victims of a Humanitarian Program

The women killed and injured in the blast were participants in a street-cleaning initiative organized under the United Nations World Food Program. The program was designed to provide vulnerable Somali women with food assistance in exchange for their labor, offering a lifeline to families struggling amid the country's protracted conflict and economic hardship. The tragic irony of the attack—that women seeking to earn food for their families through community service became victims of targeted violence—has drawn widespread condemnation and underscored the precarious situation facing civilians trying to access humanitarian aid in Mogadishu.

## Conflicting Claims Over Responsibility

In the aftermath of the bombing, responsibility for the attack has become a matter of dispute and political finger-pointing. Mogadishu's recently dismissed mayor placed blame squarely on the Islamic Courts Union (ICU), accusing the group of orchestrating the attack. However, the leader of the Islamic Courts Union firmly denied any involvement in the bombing, instead turning the accusation back on the Somali transitional government, suggesting that officials within the government may have been responsible for the attack. This exchange of accusations has left the true perpetrators of the bombing unconfirmed, adding another layer of uncertainty to an already volatile security situation.

## Context of Ongoing Conflict

The bombing did not occur in isolation but rather amid a broader pattern of violence gripping Mogadishu. Ethiopian troops, deployed in support of Somalia's internationally recognized transitional government, have been engaged in sustained clashes with Islamist insurgents linked to the Islamic Courts Union and allied groups. This conflict has transformed large parts of the capital into a battleground, with civilians frequently caught in the crossfire of military operations, roadside bombings, and other forms of insurgent attacks. The targeting of the street-cleaning program fits into this larger context of instability, where even humanitarian efforts are not immune from the violence.

## Deepening Political Crisis

Compounding the security crisis, Somalia's political leadership has been thrown into further disarray. Two-thirds of the country's government ministers have resigned in protest, leveling serious accusations against Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade. The ministers accused the prime minister of exhibiting dictatorial tendencies, citing his unilateral dismissal of Mogadishu's mayor as a key example of what they characterized as an authoritarian style of governance. This mass resignation represents a significant blow to the transitional government's stability and cohesion at a moment when unified leadership is critical to addressing both the security crisis and the humanitarian needs of the Somali population.

The convergence of this bombing, the disputed claims of responsibility, and the unraveling of the government's internal unity paints a troubling picture of a nation struggling to achieve stability amid competing military, political, and humanitarian pressures.

# Deadly Blast Strikes Food-for-Work Program in Mogadishu

A devastating roadside bomb ripped through a group of women street cleaners on Mogadishu's Maka Al Mukarama Road on Wednesday, killing at least 21 people and wounding 46 others in one of the deadliest attacks to hit Somalia's capital in recent months. The victims were participating in a United Nations World Food Program initiative that provided food rations to residents in exchange for cleaning debris and garbage from the city's war-torn streets—a program designed to offer both humanitarian relief and a measure of dignity to Mogadishu's impoverished population.

The explosion detonated without warning as the women worked along the roadside, transforming what should have been a modest effort at community rebuilding into a scene of carnage. Bodies and wounded survivors littered the street in the aftermath, as shocked residents and emergency responders scrambled to assist the injured amid the chaos and confusion that followed.

In the hours after the attack, responsibility remained fiercely contested. The Islamic Courts Union, the Islamist movement that has waged an insurgency against Somalia's transitional government and its Ethiopian military backers, denied any involvement in the bombing, suggesting instead that government forces or their allies may have been responsible. Somali government officials, meanwhile, pointed fingers at the Islamist insurgents, accusing them of deliberately targeting civilians engaged in humanitarian work as part of a broader campaign to destabilize the capital and undermine relief efforts. The competing claims left the true perpetrators unclear, adding another layer of uncertainty to an already murky and volatile conflict.

The bombing arrives at a particularly precarious moment for Mogadishu, a city that has been engulfed in near-constant violence since Ethiopian troops intervened at the end of last year to help oust the Islamic Courts Union from power and install Somalia's internationally recognized but weak transitional government. Since then, Islamist insurgents and their sympathizers have waged a persistent guerrilla campaign against Ethiopian forces and government installations, employing roadside bombs, mortar attacks, and ambushes that have killed hundreds of civilians and displaced hundreds of thousands more from their homes.

Compounding the security crisis is a deepening political rift within the transitional government itself. In recent weeks, roughly two-thirds of the cabinet's ministers have resigned en masse, citing frustration with the leadership and policies of the prime minister. This wave of resignations has thrown the fragile government into further disarray, raising serious questions about its capacity to govern effectively, maintain any semblance of security, or negotiate a path toward stability at a moment when unified leadership is desperately needed.

Taken together, the attack on the street cleaners, the unresolved question of who orchestrated it, and the political turmoil consuming the transitional government paint a grim picture of a capital city spiraling deeper into chaos. For ordinary Mogadishu residents—many of whom had turned to programs like the World Food Program's food-for-work initiative simply to survive—the bombing serves as a stark and painful reminder that even efforts to rebuild and sustain daily life amid the wreckage of war can become targets in Somalia's seemingly intractable cycle of violence.

# Somalia's Capital City: A Historical and Modern Perspective

Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia, has long been a focal point for international news coverage, with outlets like CNN regularly reporting on developments in the region. Located along the Indian Ocean coast, Mogadishu has a rich history dating back centuries as an important trading port connecting East Africa with the Arabian Peninsula, Persia, and beyond.

## Historical Significance

Once known as the "White Pearl of the Indian Ocean," Mogadishu was renowned for its stunning architecture, bustling markets, and cultural diversity. The city flourished as a center of Islamic scholarship and commerce, with influences from Arab, Persian, and various African cultures blending to create a unique urban identity.

## Challenges and Recovery

In recent decades, Mogadishu has faced significant challenges, including civil conflict and political instability that have drawn extensive international media attention. CNN, along with other major news networks, has covered various aspects of Somalia's situation, including:

- Humanitarian crises and famine relief efforts
- Security operations against extremist groups
- Political transitions and governance efforts
- Reconstruction and development initiatives

## Signs of Progress

Despite the challenges highlighted in international media, Mogadishu has shown resilience. Recent years have seen:

- Infrastructure rebuilding efforts
- Growing business activity and returning diaspora investment
- Improvements in security in certain areas
- Educational institutions reopening and expanding

## Media Coverage and Perception

International coverage from networks like CNN plays a crucial role in shaping global perceptions of Somalia. While news often focuses on conflict and crisis, there's increasing recognition of the need for more nuanced reporting that captures both the challenges and the genuine progress being made by Somali citizens, government institutions, and international partners working toward stability and development.

The story of Mogadishu continues to evolve, reflecting broader themes of resilience, recovery, and the complex path toward lasting peace and prosperity in the Horn of Africa.

counterfactuals.output:
# Roadside Bomb Kills Street Cleaners in Mogadishu, Officials Say

**Mogadishu, Somalia** — A roadside bomb ripped through a group of municipal street cleaners in the Somali capital early Tuesday, killing at least seven women and wounding a dozen others in an attack that local officials condemned as a deliberate strike on civilians.

The explosion occurred around 6:30 a.m. local time as the women, employed by Mogadishu's municipal sanitation department, were sweeping a road in the Hodan district ahead of the morning commute. Witnesses said the device had been buried in the road overnight and was likely detonated remotely as the group passed.

"They were just doing their job, cleaning the street like they do every morning," said Halima Abdi, a shopkeeper who witnessed the aftermath. "I heard the blast and ran outside. There was dust everywhere, and I saw the women — some of them were not moving. It was horrible. These are poor women trying to earn a living for their families."

Ambulances rushed to the scene, and the wounded were taken to nearby Madina and Digfer hospitals. A hospital official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to media, said several of the injured were in critical condition and that the death toll could rise.

Mogadishu Mayor's spokesperson Abdirahman Yusuf condemned the attack, calling it "a cowardly and cold-blooded act against innocent, hardworking women who posed no threat to anyone."

"These women wake up before dawn to clean the streets of this city so that others can live in dignity," Yusuf said. "To target them is to target the very soul of Mogadishu."

No group had immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, but roadside bombings in the Somali capital have frequently been attributed to al-Shabab, the al-Qaeda-linked militant group that has waged an insurgency against the Somali government for more than a decade. The group has previously targeted security forces, government convoys, and public infrastructure, though attacks striking civilian laborers have drawn particular outrage.

A police officer at the scene, Captain Mohamed Nur, said investigators believed the device was remotely detonated rather than triggered by a vehicle, suggesting the attackers may have been watching the road and chose to strike when the cleaners gathered.

"This was not random," Nur said. "Whoever planted this bomb waited for people to be there. That tells you something about the intention behind it."

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud issued a statement Tuesday afternoon expressing condolences to the victims' families and vowing that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"Once again, the enemies of peace have shown their true face by attacking defenseless women who serve our communities," the statement read. "We will not be deterred. Mogadishu will continue to rebuild, and its streets will continue to be cleaned by these brave women who symbolize our resilience."

Residents in Hodan district described a mood of grief mixed with anger. Many of the women killed were reportedly the primary breadwinners for their families, earning modest wages through a municipal employment program aimed at supporting vulnerable women in the city.

"My sister was one of them," said Fadumo Ali, who arrived at Madina Hospital searching for information about her sibling. "She left home this morning to go to work, just like every day. Now I don't know if she's alive. What did she do to deserve this?"

The attack is the latest in a series of bombings to strike Mogadishu in recent months, as Somali security forces, backed by African Union troops, continue operations against al-Shabab in rural areas outside the capital. Despite military gains reported by the government, the militant group has retained the capacity to strike within the city itself, often using improvised explosive devices planted along roadsides.

Local aid organizations called for increased protections for municipal workers and greater investment in explosive detection efforts along frequently used routes.

As of Tuesday evening, Somali police said an investigation into the bombing was ongoing, and a curfew was briefly imposed in parts of Hodan district as security forces searched for suspects.

The names of the victims had not yet been released pending notification of their families.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Deadly Bombing Strikes UN-Backed Program in Somalia, Killing Dozens

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A suicide bombing targeting participants in a UN-backed street cleaning and job creation program killed and wounded dozens of people in Mogadishu on [day], in one of the deadliest attacks to hit the war-torn capital in recent months.

## The Attack

According to local officials and hospital sources, the explosion occurred as workers gathered for the labor-intensive sanitation program, which was designed to provide temporary employment for unemployed youth while improving public health conditions in the debris-strewn capital. Witnesses described chaotic scenes as emergency responders rushed to the site amid casualties.

Preliminary reports indicate the death toll includes both program participants and bystanders, with the wounded overwhelming local medical facilities that already struggle with limited resources and years of conflict-related strain. Officials cautioned that casualty figures could rise as the full extent of injuries becomes clear.

No group had immediately claimed responsibility, though suspicion has fallen on al-Shabab, the al-Qaeda-linked militant group that has waged a long insurgency against Somalia's Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and has previously targeted civilian gatherings, government installations, and African Union peacekeepers.

## Political Reactions

The attack drew swift condemnation from Somali officials and international partners. Government representatives characterized the bombing as an attempt to undermine reconstruction efforts and sow fear among civilians participating in UN-supported livelihood programs.

United Nations officials expressed outrage, emphasizing that the street cleaning initiative was a humanitarian and development effort aimed at ordinary Somalis struggling with unemployment and the degraded infrastructure resulting from prolonged conflict. Aid organizations warned that such attacks on civilian-focused programs could jeopardize future assistance efforts in a country heavily dependent on international support.

Regional analysts suggested the bombing reflects al-Shabab's broader strategy of discouraging cooperation between Somali civilians and the TFG, as well as its Ethiopian military backers, by demonstrating that even non-military, community-based initiatives are not safe from attack.

## Background: Ethiopian Military Presence

The bombing comes against the backdrop of a controversial and increasingly strained security situation in Somalia. Ethiopian troops entered the country in late 2006 to support the TFG against the Islamic Courts Union (ICU), which had taken control of Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia earlier that year. The intervention successfully removed the ICU from power but triggered a persistent insurgency led by al-Shabab, a more radical offshoot that emerged from the ICU's collapse.

Ethiopia's continued military presence has remained deeply unpopular among many Somalis, who view it as a foreign occupation exacerbating the conflict rather than resolving it. Critics argue the Ethiopian intervention, while initially framed as a stabilizing force, has fueled anti-government sentiment and provided al-Shabab with a rallying cause for recruitment.

The African Union has maintained a peacekeeping mission (AMISOM) to bolster the TFG, though force levels have historically fallen short of mandated troop commitments, leaving security gaps that insurgents have exploited.

## Outlook

The bombing underscores the precarious security environment facing humanitarian and development efforts in Somalia, where aid workers, government employees, and ordinary civilians remain vulnerable to attack. As the TFG continues to rely on Ethiopian and African Union military support, analysts warn that until a durable political settlement is reached, both civilian infrastructure projects and international assistance programs will likely remain targets for insurgent violence.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

---
*Note: This report reflects a composite/generalized account of the type of attacks that occurred in Mogadishu during the 2007-2009 period of Ethiopian military presence. For specific casualty figures, dates, and official statements regarding an actual historical incident, please consult contemporaneous news archives from outlets such as Reuters, AP, or BBC.*

# Fighting Erupts in Mogadishu as Rival Factions Trade Blame

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP)** — Heavy fighting broke out in several districts of the Somali capital this week, killing at least a dozen people and wounding dozens more, as the country's fragile Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and remnants of the Islamic Courts Union (ICU) traded accusations over who bears responsibility for the renewed bloodshed.

Witnesses reported mortar fire and heavy machine-gun exchanges near the Bakara Market, one of Mogadishu's most volatile commercial districts, an area that has repeatedly served as a flashpoint for clashes between government forces, allied militias, and insurgents linked to the ICU's armed remnants, including elements associated with al-Shabab.

"We heard explosions from early morning until past midnight," said one resident reached by telephone, who declined to be named citing fears for his safety. "Shells landed on houses. We don't know who is fighting whom anymore — we just know we are the ones dying."

## Blame Game Intensifies

Government spokesmen accused "remnants of the Islamic Courts" of orchestrating the violence in a bid to destabilize the TFG and reassert control over the capital, which the ICU briefly governed in 2006 before being driven out.

"These are terrorist elements who refuse to accept the legitimate authority of the transitional government," a government military official told reporters, blaming insurgents for initiating mortar attacks on government positions.

Figures associated with the courts' political wing, however, rejected the characterization, accusing government troops and allied Ethiopian forces of indiscriminate shelling of civilian neighborhoods.

"The government and its foreign backers are the ones bringing war to our people," said a statement attributed to a spokesman sympathetic to the ICU cause, referring to the continued presence of Ethiopian military advisers and troops supporting the TFG. "They invaded our country and now they blame us for defending ourselves."

Independent verification of specific claims from either side remains difficult. Journalists' access to front-line areas is severely restricted, and both the TFG and ICU-aligned factions have histories of disputing casualty figures and responsibility for attacks.

## Roots in the 2006 Ethiopian Invasion

The current violence traces back to the dramatic events of December 2006, when Ethiopian forces, backing the internationally recognized but weak Transitional Federal Government, launched a rapid military campaign against the Islamic Courts Union.

The ICU had taken control of Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia earlier that year, filling a power vacuum left by more than a decade of state collapse and warlord rule following the ouster of dictator Siad Barre in 1991. The Courts brought a measure of order to the capital — reopening the airport and seaport and reducing roadblocks run by rival militias — but alarmed neighboring Ethiopia and the United States, which accused the movement's leadership of harboring al-Qaida-linked operatives and harboring ambitions to create a hardline Islamist state in the Horn of Africa.

With tacit U.S. support, Ethiopian troops crossed the border in force in late December 2006, employing air power, armor, and artillery against ICU positions. Addis Ababa framed the intervention as a preemptive strike against a hostile Islamist force on its border; Somali and international critics characterized it as an occupation driven by longstanding Ethiopian-Somali rivalry and by Washington's global campaign against Islamist militancy.

The Courts' conventional forces collapsed within days, and its leadership fled or dispersed, allowing the TFG — until then confined to the provincial town of Baidoa — to enter Mogadishu under Ethiopian protection. But the swift military victory did not translate into political stability.

## An Insurgency Takes Root

In the months since Ethiopian tanks rolled into the capital, an insurgency drawing on remnants of the Islamic Courts, allied clan militias, and a hardening faction known as al-Shabab has mounted an escalating campaign of ambushes, roadside bombings, and mortar attacks against Ethiopian and TFG forces.

Mogadishu residents have borne the brunt of the fighting. The United Nations and humanitarian organizations have repeatedly warned of a deepening crisis, with tens of thousands of people fleeing the city amid intense urban combat, and aid agencies citing acute shortages of food, medicine, and clean water in displacement camps ringing the capital.

The TFG, led by President Abdullahi Yusuf, a former warlord with deep ties to Ethiopia, has struggled to extend genuine authority beyond areas held by Ethiopian troops and African Union peacekeepers, whose deployment under the AMISOM mandate has been slow and undermanned relative to the scale of the conflict.

Critics, including some regional analysts and opposition politicians, argue the Ethiopian intervention — rather than neutralizing the Islamist threat — fragmented the ICU into more radical splinter factions, with al-Shabab in particular hardening into a more militant, transnational insurgency less amenable to negotiation than the original Courts leadership.

## No End in Sight

As of this week's clashes, there is no indication of an imminent ceasefire. Efforts at reconciliation talks, periodically floated by regional bodies including the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the African Union, have yielded little concrete progress, hampered by mutual distrust and the fragmentation of the ICU's former leadership into rival camps — some open to political dialogue, others committed to continued armed struggle.

For ordinary Mogadishu residents, the dispute over blame offers little comfort.

"Both sides say it is the other's fault," said a shopkeeper in the Bakara district whose stall was damaged in the latest fighting. "Meanwhile our children cannot go to school, and we do not know if our roofs will still be standing tomorrow."

*This report includes information gathered from local witnesses, government and ICU-affiliated statements, and background from humanitarian and regional monitoring sources. Casualty figures could not be independently confirmed.*

# Bombing Rocks Mogadishu Amid Fragile Peace Efforts

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A powerful explosion tore through a busy area of Somalia's capital this week, killing and wounding a number of civilians in an attack that underscores the fragility of the country's peace process even as diplomatic efforts continue to try to end nearly two decades of conflict.

The blast, which local witnesses described as striking without warning amid crowds of shoppers and passersby, has not yet been claimed by any group, though suspicion has fallen on militant factions opposed to Somalia's transitional government and its international backers. Somali security forces sealed off the area in the aftermath, and hospitals in the city reported an influx of casualties, further straining medical facilities already stretched thin by years of chronic instability.

## A Peace Process Under Strain

The attack comes at a delicate moment for Somalia, where the internationally backed Djibouti Agreement — signed in 2008 between the Transitional Federal Government and moderate opposition figures, including elements of the Alliance for the Re-liberation of Somalia — was intended to pave the way toward reconciliation, a ceasefire, and the eventual withdrawal of foreign troops. The accord raised hopes that Somalia might finally turn a corner after years of factional warfare, famine, and the collapse of central authority following the ouster of Siad Barre in 1991.

Yet implementation of the Djibouti framework has been halting at best. Hardline insurgent groups, most notably al-Shabab, rejected the agreement outright and have continued to wage an insurgency aimed at toppling the government and expelling African Union peacekeeping forces. Mogadishu itself remains divided, with government-held districts existing uneasily alongside areas contested or controlled by militants. Bombings, assassinations, and mortar attacks have become grim fixtures of daily life, each one chipping away at public confidence that the peace process can hold.

Analysts note that such attacks are often timed to disrupt political momentum — whether ahead of parliamentary sessions, troop deployments, or renewed diplomatic talks — and this latest bombing is likely to reinforce fears that spoilers on the ground remain both willing and able to derail negotiations pursued in Djibouti and other international venues.

## A Humanitarian Emergency Deepens

Beyond the immediate carnage, the bombing highlights a broader humanitarian catastrophe that has enveloped Somalia for years. The United Nations and aid organizations have repeatedly warned that the country is facing one of the world's most severe displacement crises, with hundreds of thousands of people forced from their homes by fighting in and around Mogadishu alone. Many now live in makeshift camps on the capital's outskirts or have fled toward the Kenyan and Ethiopian borders, where overstretched refugee camps struggle to absorb new arrivals.

Chronic insecurity has also crippled the delivery of food aid and medical supplies, with humanitarian convoys frequently targeted or blocked, and aid workers themselves increasingly at risk of kidnapping or attack. Combined with recurring drought conditions in the Horn of Africa, the violence has pushed large segments of the Somali population toward malnutrition and dependence on international relief — assistance that is often delayed or diminished precisely because of the same instability the aid is meant to help alleviate.

## International Reaction

Diplomats involved in shepherding the Djibouti process have condemned the bombing and reiterated calls for all parties to abide by ceasefire commitments, though such appeals have done little to stem the violence in the past. The African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), tasked with protecting transitional institutions and key infrastructure, faces continued pressure over its limited capacity to secure the capital, while troop-contributing nations weigh the risks of expanding their commitment against the reality of a conflict that shows few signs of abating.

For ordinary Somalis, the attack is yet another reminder of the gap between the promises made in international conference halls and the lived reality of life in Mogadishw — a city where peace deals are signed abroad while bombs continue to fall at home.

*This report reflects developments as of press time; the death toll and details surrounding the attack may be subject to revision as further information emerges.*
